weeks.title: How People Learn
weeks.objective: Use what science says about memory and learning.

slides.title: Memory and Practice
slides.body: Learning sticks when students actively recall it, spread practice out over time and connect new ideas to what they know.
bullets: Retrieval practice: quizzing beats re-reading
Spaced practice: review after a day, a week, a month
Interleaving: mix problem types
Explain it simply: if you can't, you don't understand it yet
slides.takeaway: Make students pull knowledge out of their heads, again and again.

slides.title: Working Memory and Clear Explanations
slides.body: People can hold only a few new ideas at once. Great teachers break big ideas into small steps and show worked examples.
bullets: Teach one step at a time
Model it ('I do'), practise together ('we do'), then alone ('you do')
Worked examples before independent problems
Check understanding often with quick questions
slides.takeaway: Small steps, shown clearly, then practised.

lab.title: Learning Science Lab
lab.brief: Teach someone a new skill in 10 minutes using I do, we do, you do, then test them the next day with recall questions.
lab.deliverable: A short lesson plan and the test results.
lab.proTip: The next-day quiz shows what really stuck.

caseStudy.scenario: A student re-reads their notes for hours but forgets everything in the test. What should they change?

options.text: Use self-quizzing and spaced practice over several days.
options.explanation: Retrieval and spacing make memories last.

quiz.question: 'I do, we do, you do' means:

weeks.title: Planning a Great Lesson
weeks.objective: Plan lessons with a clear goal and a way to check learning.

slides.title: Start With the Goal
slides.body: Every good lesson starts with what students should be able to do by the end, then works backwards.
bullets: Learning objective: 'By the end, students can…'
Hook: a question or problem that grabs attention
Teach, practise, check
Exit ticket: a quick question to see who got it
slides.takeaway: If you can't check it, it isn't a clear objective.

slides.title: Differentiation
slides.body: Every class has students at different levels. Plan ways to support those who struggle and stretch those who fly.
bullets: Support: worked examples, word banks, smaller steps
Stretch: harder problems, 'explain why' questions
Group work with clear roles
Adjust as you go, based on what you see

lab.title: Lesson Plan Lab
lab.brief: Plan a 40-minute lesson with an objective, hook, I do, we do, you do and an exit ticket.
lab.proTip: Plan the exit ticket first: it defines success.

caseStudy.scenario: Halfway through a lesson, most students look confused. What's best?

options.text: Keep going to finish the plan.
Pause, check what's unclear, re-explain with a new example, and practise together.

quiz.question: A learning objective should be:
quiz.explanation: You should be able to check it.

weeks.title: Managing a Class and Feedback
weeks.objective: Create calm, focused classes and give feedback that improves work.

slides.title: Routines and Relationships
slides.body: Calm classrooms run on clear routines and respectful relationships, not shouting.
bullets: Set 2 or 3 clear expectations and practise them
Greet students by name
Praise specific behaviour: 'Great use of evidence, Ahmed'
Deal with problems privately and calmly
slides.takeaway: Routines prevent most problems before they start.

slides.title: Feedback That Works
slides.body: Feedback should help the student improve the next piece of work, not just grade this one.
bullets: Be specific: what's good and what to do next
Focus on 1 or 2 improvements, not 10
Give time to act on it
Praise effort and strategy, not just talent
slides.example:
Weak: 'Good essay, 7/10.'
Strong: 'Your argument is clear. Next time, back each point with a quote from the text, as you did well in paragraph 2.'
slides.takeaway: Good feedback answers 'What do I do next?'

lab.title: Feedback Lab
lab.brief: Mark three pieces of student work with specific, actionable feedback, and plan time for students to use it.
lab.proTip: Feedback nobody acts on is wasted: build in redo time.

caseStudy.scenario: A student keeps talking during your explanation. What's the best first response?

options.text: Shout at them in front of everyone.
options.explanation: Public shouting damages relationships and calm.

options.text: Calmly remind them of the expectation, privately if possible, and praise them when they focus.
options.explanation: Calm, consistent and positive works best.

quiz.question: Specific praise looks like:
options: 'Great use of evidence in your answer.'

weeks.title: Tutoring in Dubai
weeks.objective: Tutor legally, price fairly and work well with parents.

slides.title: Tutoring Legally
slides.body: Private tutoring in Dubai requires a permit. A private tutor work permit was introduced so qualified people (including school teachers, university students and other professionals) can tutor legally.
bullets: Get the private tutor work permit before taking paying students
Keep the permit valid and follow its conditions
Safeguarding: tutor children with a parent at home or in a public space
Keep records of sessions and payments
slides.takeaway: Tutor with a permit: it protects you, your students and their parents.

slides.title: Pricing and Parents
slides.body: Tutors charge per hour or per package, depending on subject, level and experience. Parents stay loyal when they see progress.
bullets: Price by subject and level; exam years cost more
Packages of 8 or 10 sessions, paid in advance
Send a short progress update to parents after each month
Agree a cancellation policy
slides.example:
A maths tutor charges AED 200 an hour.
10-session package: AED 1,800 (10% off).
8 students, 1 hour a week each: 32 sessions a month ≈ AED 6,000 to AED 6,400 a month.
slides.takeaway: Visible progress keeps students and earns referrals.

lab.title: Tutoring Business Lab
lab.brief: Plan a tutoring offer: subject, level, price, package, permit steps and a monthly parent update template.
lab.deliverable: A one-page plan and a parent update.
lab.proTip: Start with a free 15-minute assessment: it shows parents what you'll fix.

caseStudy.scenario: A parent asks you to start tutoring their child next week, but you don't have a tutoring permit yet. What do you do?

options.text: Start anyway and keep it quiet.
options.explanation: Tutoring without a permit isn't allowed.

options.text: Apply for the permit first, explain the timeline, and start once it's approved.
